title: Cooperative & Collaborative Learning

pts: Genuine cooperative learning requires that group members need each other to succeed — positive interdependence.
Without this, group work often collapses into one learner doing the task while others passively watch.
Task design (Unit 28) can build this in directly, through information distributed unevenly across group members.
points.who: David & Roger Johnson's cooperative learning research

v: A short picture story cut into four parts

items: Divide a four-picture story so that each member of a group of four holds one picture.
Learners may not show their picture; they describe it in English.
The group agrees the order of the story.
Together they write one sentence per picture to make the complete story.
Groups compare their versions with the original.
Use sentences of a paragraph, lines of a dialogue or steps of a recipe instead of pictures.
Support: a word bank on each picture card.
Challenge: one card contains a detail that contradicts the others; the group must find it.

lines: S1: In my picture, a boy is running to the bus stop.
S2: In mine, the bus is leaving. Is your boy late?
S3: Mine is first, I think. He’s sleeping and the alarm is ringing.
S4: So yours, then yours, then mine.

blocks.x: No one can complete the story alone. That is positive interdependence: learners need one another to succeed (Johnson and Johnson 2009). Distributing information unevenly is the simplest way to build it into a task (Unit 28).

body: Purpose: to show positive interdependence. Content: four learners on a bench, each holding one piece of a jigsaw puzzle; only when the pieces meet in the centre does the picture of a bus scene appear. Style: warm, clear. Board version: a square divided into four with a learner symbol at each corner.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) to print picture-story cards.

blocks.x: Pictures drawn by the teacher or cut from old textbooks.

pts: Each learner must be individually accountable for their contribution, not just the group's overall output.
Techniques like assigning distinct roles or requiring individual sub-outputs before combining them build this in.
Without individual accountability, stronger learners often absorb the workload while weaker ones disengage.

items: Give a question (for example, What three changes would make our school greener?).
Each learner writes their own ideas silently for three minutes.
In groups, each learner shares in turn; no one repeats an idea.
The group chooses its best three ideas and notes whose idea each was.
Call on any member at random to report; everyone must be ready.
Number members 1–4; roll a die to choose the reporter (Kagan’s ‘Numbered Heads Together’).
Support: sentence starters for the individual writing stage.
Challenge: learners must give a reason for each idea.

lines: My idea is similar to Priya’s, but…
Rain-water tank (Farhan). Paper recycling bin (Lakshmi). No plastic in the canteen (Deepa).

blocks.x: The written individual stage and the random reporter make each learner accountable. Stronger learners cannot carry the group, and weaker learners cannot disappear into it.

body: Purpose: to show individual accountability. Content: four learners in a group, each with a small notebook showing their own ideas, and a die in the centre showing the number 3, with learner 3 standing to report. Style: lively, fair. Board version: four boxes with numbers and a die.

items: Wheel of Names (free) to choose a reporter at random.

blocks.x: Numbered chits drawn from a box.

pts: The jigsaw technique gives each group member unique information that others need, structurally requiring genuine cooperation.
Defined roles — reporter, timekeeper, language monitor — distribute responsibility clearly within a group task.
Rotate roles across tasks so no single learner is permanently cast in the same function.

v: Four short texts on one topic (for example, four Indian scientists)

items: Form home groups of four; give each member a different text.
Learners with the same text meet in ‘expert groups’ to read, discuss and make notes.
Experts return to home groups and teach their text to the others.
The home group completes a task that needs all four texts, such as a comparison table.
Give a short individual quiz on all four texts.
In fixed benches, the front bench and back bench swap to form expert groups; home groups stay on their own bench.
Support: easier texts or a note frame for some expert groups.
Challenge: experts prepare one question to check their group’s understanding.

blocks.x: Four texts (written for this book): C. V. Raman, Janaki Ammal, Anna Mani, Satyendra Nath Bose. Expert language:

lines: My scientist was a botanist. The main thing to remember is…
Let me check: what was Anna Mani’s field?

blocks.x: Aronson developed the jigsaw classroom in the United States in the 1970s to reduce hostility between groups of learners in newly desegregated schools (Aronson et al. 1978). Each learner holds unique information, so every voice becomes necessary.

body: Purpose: to show the jigsaw structure. Content: two panels. In the first, four home groups each contain four colours. In the second, learners of the same colour meet in expert groups. Arrows show movement both ways. Style: diagrammatic. Board version: coloured chalk dots moving between circles.

items: Padlet (free plan) with one column per expert group for shared notes.

blocks.x: Printed or hand-copied texts, one colour of paper per text.

pts: Heterogeneous grouping (mixed ability, mixed background) tends to maximise the learning benefit of cooperative tasks.
This connects directly to Unit 15's differentiation principles, applied specifically to cooperative task design.
Vary composition across tasks rather than fixing groups permanently, echoing Unit 15's warning against calcified labels.

v: Class list; notes on language level, confidence and home language

items: Mark each learner on the class list with a rough level and a note on confidence.
Form mixed groups: one stronger, two middle, one weaker learner, with some language and gender diversity.
Check that no group has two very dominant or two very silent members.
Keep these groups for three or four weeks, then reorganize.
Sometimes use random or interest-based groups for variety.
Let learners choose partners for low-stakes tasks, and teacher-planned groups for major ones.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Group C: Kiran (confident, strong), Salma and Ravi (steady), Pooja (new to English, strong in Hindi). Pooja can plan in Hindi with Salma, then report one idea in English.

blocks.x: Heterogeneous groups generally benefit learning in cooperative tasks, but they must not become permanent labels. Unit 15 warns against fixed ability grouping; rotation keeps groups flexible.

body: Purpose: to show heterogeneous grouping. Content: a seating plan with coloured tiles representing different learners, arranged so that each group of four contains different colours, and a small arrow labelled ‘rotate in four weeks’. Style: tidy, colourful. Board version: not applicable.

items: Flippity random group generator (free) with a Google Sheet class list.

blocks.x: A pencil seating plan in the register.

points.h: Social Skills as a Taught Component
pts: Skills like active listening, disagreeing politely, and encouraging quieter members often need to be explicitly taught, not assumed.
A brief, explicit teaching point on one social skill per cooperative task builds this capacity over time.
This connects to Unit 24's pragmatics work — appropriate interactional behaviour varies and can be taught.

items: Choose one social skill for the task (for example, disagreeing politely).
Ask: what does it look like, and what does it sound like?
Build a T-chart with the class.
During the task, one group member notes each time the skill is used.
After the task, groups report one example.
Other skills: inviting a quiet member, summarizing, asking for clarification.
Support: the phrases in the T-chart are read aloud and practised chorally.
Challenge: learners use two different phrases for the same function.

lines: Looks like: nodding before speaking, eye contact, a calm voice.
Sounds like: I see your point, but… That’s a good idea. What about…? I’m not sure I agree, because…

blocks.x: Cooperation is not automatic; it must be taught (Johnson and Johnson 2009). This also connects to Unit 24: appropriate ways of disagreeing vary between cultures and between English and learners’ home languages.

body: Purpose: to show a social skills chart. Content: a large T-chart with drawings of listening postures on the left and speech bubbles with polite phrases on the right. Style: bright classroom poster. Board version: a T-chart in chalk.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a printed skills poster.

blocks.x: A chart-paper T-chart kept on the wall.

body: Teach one social skill at a time and keep its chart on the wall for several weeks. A skill used once is forgotten; a skill practised every week becomes part of how the class works.

pts: A brief reflection on how the group worked together, not just what they produced, builds cooperative skill over time.
This is Unit 9's reflective practice principle applied at the group, rather than individual, level.
Even two or three minutes of structured reflection meaningfully improves future group task performance.

items: At the end of the task, each group takes a card with two questions.
Groups discuss: What did we do well as a group? What will we do better next time?
One member writes the answers.
Collect the cards and read a few aloud.
Return the cards before the next group task as a reminder.
Use a quick thumbs-up/sideways/down for each member’s participation.
Support: groups answer in the home language, then choose one sentence in English.
Challenge: groups give specific examples.

lines: Well: everyone gave one idea. Better: we spoke too loudly and didn’t let Anil finish.

blocks.x: This is the reflective practice of Unit 9 applied to groups. Even two or three minutes of structured reflection helps groups work better the next time.

body: Purpose: to show group processing. Content: a small index card with two questions and handwritten answers, beside four learners leaning in to discuss it. Style: calm, reflective. Board version: two questions on the board.

items: Google Forms (free) for a quick group reflection where devices are available.

blocks.x: Small index cards kept in a group envelope.

pts: Assess both the task's product and, separately, the quality of the group's collaborative process.
This avoids rewarding one dominant contributor while other group members' cooperative effort goes unrecognised.
This previews the collaborative-assessment work coming later in this tier, at Unit 43.

items: Plan two assessment strands for a group task: product (the poster, report or presentation) and process (how the group worked).
Write three simple process criteria.
During the task, observe one or two groups per lesson using the criteria.
Add a short peer rating of each member’s contribution.
Combine product and process marks, with the process mark partly individual.
Include a brief individual written reflection on what each member contributed.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: All members contribute ideas. The group listens and builds on ideas. The group uses English for reporting and key discussions.
Rate each member from 1 (little) to 3 (a lot) for ideas, effort and listening.

blocks.x: Assessing only the product rewards a dominant member and hides the work of others. Unit 43 returns to peer and collaborative assessment.

body: Purpose: to show that product and process are both assessed. Content: a balance scale with a finished group poster on one pan and a picture of learners collaborating on the other, level. Style: clean, balanced. Board version: a simple scale.

items: Google Sheets (free) to record product and process marks.

blocks.x: A paper observation grid on a clipboard.

pts: Unstructured 'group work' without interdependence or accountability produces the free-rider problem cooperative learning is designed to prevent.
Groups too large lose the individual accountability smaller, well-structured groups maintain.
Diagnosing failure against these specific structural elements is more useful than concluding 'group work doesn't work for this class.'

v: Notes on a group task that did not work

items: Recall a group task that went badly.
Check it against the elements of this unit: interdependence, accountability, roles, composition, social skills, processing.
Identify the missing element or elements.
Redesign the task to include them.
Try the new version and compare.
Teachers exchange failed tasks in a teacher circle and redesign each other’s.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Task: groups of eight make a poster on water conservation. Problem: two learners did everything while the rest were free riders. Missing: interdependence (anyone could do the whole task), accountability (no individual part), group size (too large). Redesign: groups of four; each member researches one sub-topic; each writes and presents one section.

blocks.x: The conclusion ‘Group work doesn’t work with this class’ is rarely justified. Usually a specific element is missing.

body: Purpose: to show failure analysis. Content: a clipboard checklist of six elements, with two ticked and four with question marks, beside a redesigned group task. Style: practical. Board version: a six-item list.

items: A notes app to record diagnoses and redesigns.

body: Take one group task you plan to use next week. Before teaching it, answer two questions: Why does each learner need the others? and How will I know what each learner contributed? If you cannot answer both, redesign the task.

dek: Unit 34 of 100: closing this stretch of deep dives by turning group work from a classroom management technique into a full, evidence-based methodology.

aims.x: This unit turns group work from a management technique into a methodology. It sets out the structural elements that distinguish cooperative learning from simply putting learners in groups, and shows how each can be built into English lessons in large classes with fixed benches.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain positive interdependence and design tasks that create it;
build individual accountability into group tasks;
use jigsaw and rotating roles in an English lesson;
make principled decisions about group composition;
teach one social skill explicitly per cooperative task;
run short group-processing reflections;
assess both the product and the process of group work;
diagnose why a group task has failed.

why: Why this matters. 'Get into groups' is not the same as cooperative learning. The difference lies in deliberate structure — and that structure is what makes group work actually work.

background.x: Most teachers have given the instruction ‘Get into groups’ and watched what follows: one learner writes, one talks, and the rest wait. The problem is not group work itself but group work without structure. David and Roger Johnson, drawing on Morton Deutsch’s theory of social interdependence, spent decades studying how cooperation, competition and individual effort affect learning. Their reviews conclude that cooperative arrangements generally produce higher achievement and better relationships than competitive or individualistic ones, provided that certain conditions are met (Johnson and Johnson 1989, 2009). They name five: positive interdependence, individual accountability, promotive interaction, social skills and group processing. This unit follows those elements, adding Elliot Aronson’s jigsaw technique (Aronson et al. 1978) and the structural approach of Spencer Kagan (1994).

Cooperative learning has a special value in language classrooms. It multiplies the talk time available in a class of fifty, and group tasks create the interaction and negotiation of meaning described in Unit 30. From a sociocultural perspective, learners working together can achieve more than they could alone, and support one another within what Vygotsky (1978) called the zone of proximal development. Neomy Storch (2002) found that the pattern of interaction matters: pairs that were collaborative showed more evidence of learning than pairs in which one partner dominated. George Jacobs and colleagues (2002) and the collection edited by McCafferty, Jacobs and DaSilva Iddings (2006) show how these principles apply in second language teaching.

Indian classrooms bring both challenges and resources. Benches are fixed, classes are large, and noise travels. Yet learners are used to working together outside school, in families, teams and festival preparations, and many classrooms already use bench groups informally. NEP 2020 calls for experiential, collaborative and discussion-based learning (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020), and the NCF 2023 encourages group and peer learning (NCERT 2023). Home languages have a clear place: groups can plan in Kannada or Urdu and report in English, so that weaker learners contribute ideas as well as language.

items: Group product. A poster, report or presentation assessed with a rubric.
Process observation. Structured teacher notes on two groups per lesson.
Individual accountability. Short individual quizzes or sub-outputs after jigsaw tasks.
Peer rating. Learners rate each group member’s contribution, with teacher moderation.
What happens in your class when you say ‘Get into groups’?
Which of your group tasks have real interdependence?
How do you know what each learner contributed?
How often do your groups change?
Which social skill do your learners most need to learn?
When did you last ask a group how they worked together?

terms.def: Structured group work in which learners depend on one another to achieve a shared goal, while each remains individually accountable.
In a jigsaw activity, a group of learners who study the same text or topic together before returning to their home groups to teach it to others.
A group member who contributes little and benefits from others’ work. Cooperative learning reduces free riding through individual accountability and clear roles.
In cooperative learning, time for groups to reflect on how well they worked together and what to improve, for example at the end of a task.
Grouping learners of different abilities, backgrounds or languages together so that they can support and learn from each other, as in many cooperative learning structures.
In cooperative learning, the principle that each member is responsible for their own learning and contribution, checked for example by an individual quiz after group work.
A cooperative structure in which each group member studies a different part of the material in an expert group, then teaches it to their home group, so that all parts are needed to complete the task.
In cooperative learning, a condition in which group members need one another to succeed, so that each member’s contribution matters (Johnson and Johnson 1989).
In cooperative learning, face-to-face interaction in which group members help, encourage and explain to one another (Johnson and Johnson 1989).

In cooperative learning, the interpersonal skills needed for group work, such as listening, taking turns, encouraging others and disagreeing politely. Johnson and Johnson (1989) argue these must be taught explicitly, not assumed.
